item.title: Brazil picks 27 critical minerals in push for local supply chain
item.description: New classification will steer public funding toward domestic processing and projects considered vital to industrial growth.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
Brazil picks 27 critical minerals in push for local supply chain

Marina Meireles | November 8, 2026 | 11:37 am Critical Minerals   Exploration   Regulatory Issues   Latin America   Aluminum   Chrome   Cobalt   Copper   Gold   Graphite   Iron Ore   Lithium   Manganese   Molybdenum   Nickel   Palladium   Platinum   Rare Earth   Rare Earths   Tin   Tungsten   Uranium   Vanadium   Zinc

Caldeira rare earth project location. ( Image courtesy of Meteoric Resources | Facebook. )

Brazil has designated 27 critical minerals as the country looks to accelerate mineral projects, develop the sector domestically and reduce its reliance on exporting raw materials.

The National Council for Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE) approved the list on Nov. 5, dividing the minerals into three priority groups based on their importance to national security, industrial development and supply chain resilience. The classification will help determine which mining projects qualify for federal support.

“For so long we have exported mineral wealth as ore and imported it back as a finished product, developing value and jobs in other countries,” development, industry, commerce and services minister, Brazil’s minister of development, industry, commerce and services, Márcio Elias Rosa, said. “We want to stop this cycle and create a strategy to develop this here.”

The initiative comes as countries seek to diversify supplies of minerals essential to electric vehicles, renewable energy, defence and advanced technologies.

Brazil hopes to capture more value from its mineral resources by encouraging investment in refining and manufacturing rather than relying primarily on raw material exports.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said the government intends to work with international partners rather than control the industry outright.

“We don’t want the state to have absolute control over exploration, processing and industrialization,” Lula said during the council meeting, according to Bloomberg. “We need to work with other countries that want to join us in developing and processing this wealth.”

Only the 27 minerals included in the list, and nationally registered projects, will be eligible to receive government support, according to the new government strategy.

The list

The council identified nine high-priority minerals: rare earths, graphite, lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese, silicon and uranium. The government said high-priority minerals have a high geopolitical risk, global demand and low substitution rate for other materials, CNN Brasil reported .

“The list will function as the compass of Brazilian mineral politics, giving the sector the most important tool: predictability,” the mines and energy ministry said in a statement to G1 .

Eight minerals fall into the medium-priority category: tungsten, chrome, vanadium, tantalum, titanium, phosphate, potassium and sulfur. The remaining 10 are classified as lower priority: niobium, tin, iron, zinc, gold, magnesium, molybdenum, thorium, aluminum and platinum group metals.

The classifications will undergo reviews every four years to account for economic, technological and geopolitical developments.

Investment priority

Having this list will allow the government to direct financing toward projects that strengthen domestic mineral production and processing. The rules for approval or denial of projects still need to be defined.

The council also created a fund to reduce risks and expand investments in the sector, known as FGAM. It can receive up to R$2 billion (about $364 million) from the federal government as well as more from local and state governments and private investment.

A separate Federal Program for Critical and Strategic Minerals (PFMCE) will have an annual funding limit of R$1 billion ($180 million) between 2030 and 2034 so companies can invest in mining development and transformation.

The measures follow Lula’s approval in September of R$5 billion (about $909 million) in funding to advance rare earths exploration, part of Brazil’s broader push to develop its mineral industry.

Lula’s Brazil win puts rare earths in Trump’s crosshairs

Both the council and government aim to have another meeting on this issue before the end of the year to better define supply chain priorities to advance investment decisions in the sector.

The list will be reassessed every four years and may undergo changes based on economical, technological or geopolitical changes across the globe.

(With files from Bloomberg)

item.title: Ontario’s Lecce warns that Democrats offer no tariff cure
item.description: Canada shouldn’t expect the United States to lift tariffs simply because Democrats won control of Congress, Ontario Energy and Mines Minister said.
item.dc:creator: Northern Miner Staff
item.content:encoded:
Ontario’s Lecce warns that Democrats offer no tariff cure

Frédéric Tomesco | November 5, 2026 | 4:00 pm Regulatory Issues   Canada   USA   Aluminum   Copper   Nickel

Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce (in a file photo) says Canada still faces U.S. protectionism regardless of the midterm elections. Credit: The Northern Miner

Canada shouldn’t expect the United States to lift tariffs simply because Democrats won control of Congress , Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said.

Speaking two days after the U.S. midterm elections, Lecce said the outcome could strengthen Prime Minister Mark Carney’s negotiating position. Still, protectionism runs through both major U.S. political parties, which will leave Canadian exporters exposed even after President Donald Trump leaves office, he cautioned.

“I’m just not convinced it materially changes our fundamental reality on the ground,” Lecce said of the U.S. midterm election results in a lunchtime speech Thursday to the Empire Club of Toronto. “The change of the composition of Congress doesn’t change the policy position of America vis-a-vis tariffs.”

Lecce’s remarks underscore the gap between securing a trade agreement and eliminating tariffs. For Canadian metals producers, a trade deal may offer greater certainty without removing the tariffs that raise the cost of selling into the U.S. market.

Lame-duck Trump

Democrats won both the House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday’s elections, giving them power to challenge Trump’s agenda when the new Congress convenes in January. The results leave the Republican president facing an opposition-controlled Congress for his final two years in office.

While U.S. political analysts pointed to voter frustration over high prices, the Iran war and government corruption as key factors behind Tuesday’s outcome, Lecce insists trade friction with Canada figured prominently in the campaign.

“Tariffs were on the ballot,” he said. “We stayed in our lane, but it’s clear that Canada was on the ballot.”

New momentum

Negotiations between the neighbours and trading partners have been showing fresh momentum. Carney said Tuesday that Washington had dropped demands affecting Canada’s ability to negotiate agreements with other countries. Trump, meanwhile, said a deal was close, Reuters reported.

Carney’s recent comments on the state of talks are “a good signal,” Lecce said. The Democrats’ win Tuesday “perhaps will enable a better hand for Prime Minister Carney and the national government to land a deal.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford should get credit for pressing Carney to reject an earlier agreement that would have entrenched tariffs, Lecce added.

Recounting a conversation between the two leaders, Lecce said Ford told Carney this summer: “’Do not sign a bad deal that will lock us and create the precedent of acceptance of tariffs in perpetuity. No deal is materially better than a good deal.”

Ford also made it clear to Carney that Ontario would oppose the deal publicly, according to Lecce.

Wider dispute

Ottawa suspended negotiations with the U.S. in August. Washington subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on $27.6 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian countermeasures .

The dispute extends beyond those measures. According to Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service, U.S. sectoral tariffs on covered steel, aluminum and copper products range from 15% to 50%, subject to product and content rules. Certain other tariffs apply even when Canadian goods qualify for preferential treatment under the continental trade agreement.

The bilateral talks are unfolding alongside negotiations over the Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement, or CUSMA. The pact replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement in July 2020, following renegotiation during Trump’s first presidency.

Washington declined to extend CUSMA in its current form at the July 1 review. That triggered annual reviews rather than immediate expiry: the agreement’s existing term runs to 2036, and the three countries can jointly approve another 16-year term.

Canada has explicitly linked those discussions to relief from sectoral tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber. Preserving CUSMA and resolving the tariff dispute therefore remain connected negotiating objectives.

Diversification

Even as efforts advance to rebuild the American relationship, Canada and Ontario should continue to deepen ties with other nations, Lecce argued.

“We should strengthen that relationship [with the U.S.], get it back on track, but be very vigorous in diversification,” he said. Ontario’s goal is “to make sure we are less exposed, less shocked by that vulnerability when conservatively, well over 75% of our trade is going to one nation.”

Even so, “it doesn’t mean that we can’t hope for some return to what I’d call just normal, respectful civil dialog with the most foundational relationship on earth, which is the United States.”

item.title: AngloGold plans $900 million mine expansion amid stronger profit
item.description: The investment comes as the gold miner aims to incrementally increase production by the end of the decade.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
AngloGold plans $900 million mine expansion amid stronger profit

Marina Meireles | November 5, 2026 | 9:55 am Top Companies   Africa   Latin America   Gold

Geita open pit mine, located in northwestern Tanzania, is AngloGold’s largest single gold mining operation. ( Image: AngloGold Ashanti )

AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU) plans to invest up to $900 million in expanding brownfield operations across its portfolio, targeting a production increase of 300,000 ounces to 450,000 ounces by 2030.

The investments will focus on the Geita gold mine in Tanzania, Siguiri in Guinea and Cuiabá in Brazil, as well as the ongoing ramp-up at Obuasi in Ghana. The company expects the projects to generate real internal rates of return exceeding 35%, Reuters reported.

“These are high-return, capital efficient projects at our operating mines that are expected to provide high-margin ounces and unlock further value from our portfolio,” AngloGold Ashanti CEO Alberto Calderon said in a statement.

The plan is to use existing infrastructure and operational footprints to reduce risk and optimize capital intensity.

Geita will receive the larger portion of the funding, up to $580 million to raise output to 600,000 ounces by 2030. Cuiabá’s expansion will cost between $200 million and $250 million, adding about 75,000 ounces to its output.

Another $70 million will be put towards the Suguiri mine, looking to add another 100,000 ounces to its production.

Shares in AngloGold Ashanti were up 0.35% to $88.22 apiece by mid-day Thursday in New York, valuing the company at $44.6 billion.

Profit on the rise

AngloGold reported a 12% increase for its EBITDA for Q3 2026 to $1,568 million, from $1,400 million for Q3 2025.

The company said on its Q3 earnings release that the growth is supported by the increase in the average gold price received per ounce to $4,239/oz, from $3,490/oz in the same period in 2025.

AngloGold Ashanti said its full year gold production guidance of 2,800,000 ounces to 3,170,000 ounces is reaffirmed.

Its gold production was about 3.65% more costly than the previous quarter, at $1,534 per ounce due gold royalties and higher fuel costs.

The company also reported that a worker died due to a rockfall at the Sukari underground mine in August 2026. Operations were suspended while investigations took place, but have since resumed.

(With files from Reuters)
